Abstract—A large proportion of the Bayesian mechanism
design literature is restricted to the family of regular distributions
Freg [Mye81] or the family of monotone hazard rate (MHR)
distributions FMHR [BMP63], which has overshadowed this rich
and well-developed theory. We (re-)introduce two generalized
families: quasi-regular distributions FQ-reg and quasi-MHR distributions FQ-MHR . Altogether, these four families form the following
hierarchy:

Approximation by Bayesian Simple Mechanisms: By
a line of works initiated by Hartline and Roughgarden [HR09a], mechanisms with elementary rules already
can attain constant approximations [HR09a], [CHMS10],
[CEG+ 10], [Yan11], [Ala14], [CFK14], [DFK16], [AHN+ 19],
[CFH+ 21], [JLTX20], [JLQ+ 19b], [JLQ19a], [JJLZ22],
[GPZ21], [BGL+ 21], [JMZ22], [PT22], [BC23].
For example, Bayesian Optimal Uniform Pricing,2 which
arguably is the most straightforward and practical mechanism,
achieves a tight ≈ 0.3817-approximation to the optimal mechanism, Bayesian Myerson Auction [AHN+ 19], [JLTX20],
[JLQ+ 19b].

Secondly, they satisfy natural mathematical properties (about

of these extensions incur no quantitative loss, or even improve
the state of the art for the original families. Finally, beyond the

revenue maximization for symmetric versus asymmetric regular

(less-than-)one-sample prophet inequalities, respectively. To the

Specifically, the TCS community has brought/renewed several

on approximation guarantees, (ii) simplicity of mechanism
rules, and (iii) robustness to information assumptions. (See
the surveys [HR09b], [CS14], [Rou14], [Luc17], [JLQ+ 19c],

The above issues overshadow the whole theory of Bayesian
mechanism design. To the rescue, we shall go beyond regularity/MHR and seek their appropriate relaxations/surrogates.
(Alas, there are very few previous works from this perspective.5 ) In this manner, we will strengthen applicability of the
whole theory and, conversely, better reveal essence thereof.
Before all else, we shall stipulate criteria for plausible new
conditions.
1) The new conditions shall be as general as possible
– cover regularity/MHR at least – but still involve “a
certain degree of regularity” so as to enable extensions
of previous results.
2) The new conditions must involve strong economic intuition, à la regularity/MHR.6
3) Ideally, the new conditions shall also be mathematically
natural and elegant.
Seeking such conditions and (nontrivially) generalizing previous results are the themes of our work.

The Sample Complexity of Revenue Maximization: By a
line of works initiated by Cole and Roughgarden [CR14],
a polynomial number of samples is already sufficient for
an empirical (1 − ε)-approximation of Bayesian Myerson
Auction [MR15], [CGM15], [MM16], [DHP16], [RS16],
[GN17], [Syr17], [GHZ19b], [HT19], [CHMY23], [LSTW23],
[JLX23], [CJLZ25]. Although these results are central in the
whole discipline, alas, they all require value distributions to
satisfy the (relatively weaker) regularity condition [Mye81] or
the (relatively stronger) monotone hazard rate (MHR) condition [BMP63].4 Yet without any distributional assumption, on
the contrary, no meaningful result would be possible.
Although regularity/MHR are very standard conditions in
the literature, we must look forward to extensions of the above
results under much weaker conditions (if possible), especially
with regard to the “robustness to information assumptions”
principle. Namely, irregular/non-MHR distributions are ordinary in practice. E.g., the equal-revenue distribution – a
paradigmatic regular distribution – would be irregular after
slight change F1 (v) = (1−1/v)·1[v ≥ 2]. I.e., a random value
v1 ∼ F1 almost follows the equal-revenue distribution, except
for a minimum possible value of 2 instead of 1. Likewise, the
exponential distribution – a paradigmatic MHR distribution
– would be irregular and thus non-MHR after slight change
F2 (v) = (1 − e−v ) · 1[v ≥ 1].11 All mentioned results and
many others, which are shown under regularity/MHR, cannot
accommodate such ordinary distributions.
▷ In online advertising, consortia in Google’s Open Bidding
aggregate bids from multiple advertisers to participate in realtime auctions. The consortium submits a single bid equal to
the maximum of its members’ private valuations for an ad impression. Suppose there is a consortium with two advertisers,
with asymmetric regular value distributions F11 (v) = 1 − 1/v
for v ≥ 1 and F12 (v) = 1[v ≥ 2], respectively. Then, the
“overall” value (and bid in truthful mechanisms) distribution
would be F1 (v) = F11 (v) · F12 (v) = (1 − 1/v) · 1[v ≥ 2],
which is not regular.
▷ Carbon credit auctions exhibit similar max-based group
behavior where firms form alliances to bid for emissions
permits. Here, the group’s effective valuation is determined
by the member with the highest marginal cost of emissions
reduction, as this firm faces the steepest penalty for noncompliance. Suppose there is an alliance with two firms, with
asymmetric MHR distributions F21 (v) = 1 − e−v for v ≥ 0
and F22 (v) = 1[v ≥ 1]. Then, the “overall” value distribution
would be F2 (v) = F21 (v)·F22 (v) = (1−e−v )·1[v ≥ 1], which
is not MHR.

In this work, we initiate the study of two generalized
families: quasi-regular distributions and quasi-MHR distributions. Likewise, the parameterized families of λ-regular
(a.k.a. α-strongly regular) distributions [CR14], [SS19], which
smoothly interpolate regular distributions and MHR distributions, generalize to λ-quasi-regular distributions.
The significance of our new families is manifold. Firstly,
their defining conditions are immediate “economic” relaxations of the original defining conditions (e.g., regularity as
monotonicity of the virtual value functions), capturing key
economic intuitions. Secondly, they satisfy natural mathematical properties (about order statistics) failed for the original
families, thus technically more tractable. Thirdly, from all
four research topics mentioned at the beginning of the introduction, we extend numerous results known merely for
the original families to our new families. Many of these
extensions utilize new analysis ideas, incur no quantitative
loss, or even improve the state of the art for the original
families. Finally, beyond the third point, our new families
guide us to entirely new perspectives and thus entirely unknown results. For example, regarding revenue maximization
for symmetric versus asymmetric regular buyers, we acquire
0.5- versus 0.1908-approximations for the (less-than-)onesample prophet inequalities, respectively. To the best of our
knowledge, such results are blank in the literature, despite their
widely-studied welfare maximization counterparts [CDFS22],
[RWW20], [CCES20], [CDF+ 21], [CCES24]. Below, we explain our contributions and their connection to the literature
in details.

Revenue Maximization for Buyers with Private Budgets.
Budgeted utility is one of the most classic non-quasilinear
utility models [CG00], [PV14], [DW17], [FHL19]. Compared
with quasilinear buyers, the revenue-optimal mechanism for
private budgeted buyers is much more complicated, even for
single-buyer instances [CG00], [DW17]. Prior work [FHL19,
Theorem 5.1] shows that posting a take-it-or-leave-it price is
a 12 -approximation for single-buyer instances when the buyer
has a regular distribution. The crux of their analysis is the tail
bound of regular distributions. By showing that quasi-regular
distributions admit the same tail bound (Proposition III.5),
we can obtain an approximation-preserving generalization of
[FHL19, Theorem 5.1], from regular distributions to quasiregular distributions.

B. The Downward-Closed Settings

In this section, we study the revenue maximization problem with a single sample access. A rapidly growing literature [DRY15], [FILS15], [HMR18], [BGMM18], [DZ20],
[FHL21], [ABB22] has been established in this direction. An
important motivation in this area is to identify and characterize
the “minimum information” needed for achieving a meaningful
revenue approximation guarantee.
We focus on the single-item setting for multiple buyers.
In this model, the seller does not know the buyers’ valuation
distributions F , but has a single sample access of the first order
statistic of the valuation profile. Specifically, while neither the
valuation profile v = {vi }i∈[n] nor the valuation distributions
F = {Fi }i∈[n] is known by the seller, she has a single sample
s(1:n) ∼ F(1:n) drawn from the (unknown) first order statistic
(i.e., highest value) distribution F(1:n) and is independent with
the realized valuation profiles {vi }i∈[n] .
We remark that the single sample access of the first order
statistic can be viewed as the “minimal prior information”,
since no bounded approximation guarantee can be achieved
when the seller has no information about distributions F , or
has a sample access of k-th order statistic with k ≥ 2.
Motivated by the approximate optimality of Bayesian Optimal Uniform Pricing in the Bayesian mechanism design
setting (Theorem 5), we are interested in Identity Pricing that
posts the realized sample s(1:n) ∼ F(1:n) from the first order
statistic distribution as a take-it-or-leave-it price to all buyers.
We present revenue approximation of Identity Pricing against
both Bayesian Optimal Uniform Reserve and Bayesian
Optimal Mechanism, both of which heavily rely on the
knowledge of buyers distributions. All results in this section
are summarized in Section VII and Section VII.

In this work, we introduce the families of quasi-regular
distributions FQ-reg , and quasi-MHR distributions FQ-MHR , as
generalizations of the classic regular Freg and MHR distributions FMHR , respectively. Many structural properties of the
original distribution families Freg , FMHR , such as probability
tail bounds, extend naturally to these new families FQ-reg ,
FQ-MHR . Additionally, we demonstrate that while the original
families are closed under the operation of the “i.i.d. order
statistics” operation, the new families maintain closure under
the “order statistic” operation.
Leveraging these structural properties, we extend various important and seminal results in single-parameter revenue maximization—revenue approximation by Bayesian
simple mechanisms, by prior-independent mechanisms, by
a single sample, and the sample-complexity of revenue
maximization—to the new distribution families. Many of these
results are approximation-preserving generalizations, requiring
technically challenging analysis, and some also advance the
state-of-the-art even for the original distribution family Freg .
There are many interesting directions for future research.
First, an important next step would be to rigorously prove
all conjectures posed in this work, particularly those that
specify the tight bounds for various approximations. See
Tables I and III to V for details. Second, it would also be
worthwhile to investigate whether other important revenue
approximation results in the literature can be extended to these
new distribution families. For instance, it would be valuable
to extend the 2-approximation results of n-Duplicate VCG
Auction and Bayesian Monopoly Reserves from regular
buyers, as established in [HR09a, Theorems 3.7 and 4.4],
to quasi-regular buyers within matroid environments, and to
adapt the randomization techniques developed in [ABB22] to
improve the revenue approximation by a single sample for
quasi-regular buyers. Third, leveraging the structural results
on order statistics developed in this work, it may be possible
to achieve improved (or even tight) competition complexity
bounds [EFF+ 17] for multi-item auctions with unit-demand
buyers. Finally, it would be worthwhile to explore whether
these new distribution families exhibit additional desirable
economic and mathematical properties. For example, are the
new distribution families close under the “sum” or “i.i.d. sum”
operations?42
